html:
The Pyu city-states were a group of walled Buddhist cities in the dry zone of Upper Burma, from about the 2nd century BCE to the mid-11th century. The Pyu spoke a Tibeto-Burman language and are the earliest people of Burma whose records survive.

Their cities sat in the three irrigated rice plains of Upper Burma along the Irrawaddy River. Five large walled sites are known, among them Beikthano, Halin and Sri Ksetra. Halin was the chief city until around the 7th or 8th century; then Sri Ksetra, near modern Pyay and twice its size, took the lead. The walls enclosed rice fields as well as houses, a pattern unusual for cities of the time.

What they left:

  • Buddhist stupas, some of the oldest in Southeast Asia, and urn burials for cremated dead.
  • Inscriptions in the Pyu language written in a script from South India, along with Pali and Sanskrit texts.
  • Silver coins, and signs of trade with India and China.

Chinese records describe Pyu embassies and music in the Tang court around 800. Raids by Nanzhao, a kingdom in Yunnan, around 832 badly damaged the realm. Over the next two centuries Burman speakers settled at Pagan, and Pagan absorbed the Pyu cities and much of their culture. The Buddhism of Pagan built on Pyu foundations. Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.
